# Types of Ties and Their Graphs {#sec-ties} ## Introduction Nodes and edges are the fundamental building blocks of a graph. However, the types of relationships that the edges represent can change both how we understand the network conceptually and what mathematical techniques we can apply to the graph when computing *graph metrics* (the subject of @sec-graphmetrics). When doing social network analysis, we map our understanding of the nature of the **social relationships** we are studying to the **types of graphs** we use to represent the network formed by the **concatenation** of those relationships [@martin09]. This chapter integrates the sociological classifications of ties with their graph-theoretic representations, demonstrating how different social relations dictate the mathematical properties and structures of the networks they form. --- ## Symmetric Ties and Undirected Graphs By definition, some relations lack any inherent directionality. **Mutuality** (or **reciprocity**) is built in by construction. For example, "spending time together" or "being siblings" are relations where mutuality is logically and necessarily implied. It would be nonsensical for a person (say *A*) to claim that they spend time with another person (say *B*) and for *B* to say that they do not spend time with *A*. In social network analysis, these are called **symmetric ties** [@heider46]. Formally, if a tie is symmetric, then the existence of a tie from *A* to *B* logically implies that *B* is also tied to *A* ($AB \implies BA$). Social networks composed of symmetric ties are represented as **undirected graphs**, such as the one shown in @fig-undirected. When an undirected graph has no **loops** (edges connecting a node to itself), and there is only one edge connecting adjacent vertices to one another (the graph has no **multiedges**), it is called a **simple undirected graph**. ::: {.cell .fig-cap-location-bottom} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![An undirected graph](lesson-graphs-ties_files/figure-html/fig-undirected-1.png){#fig-undirected width=768} ::: ::: ### Real-World Examples of Symmetric Ties 1. **Similarity and Propinquity**: Two people being in the same place at the same time (co-location), or having similar socio-demographic attributes (e.g., sharing nationality or gender). 2. **Co-membership / Affiliations**: "Being in the same class as" every other student in your seminar. All **co-memberships** create symmetric ties among all involved actors (we will revisit this in @sec-affiliation). If *A* is a teammate of *B* in a soccer club, *B* is necessarily a teammate of *A*. In undirected graphs, the order in which we name the nodes in an edge does not matter ($AB$ and $BA$ refer to the exact same edge). --- ## Asymmetric Ties and Directed Graphs In contrast to co-membership or spending time together, many social relationships allow for inherent **directionality**. These are represented by **asymmetric ties** [@heider46]. For these ties, one member of a pair can claim a relationship with the other, but it is possible (though not necessary) that the other person does not send the same relationship back. Helping, texting, and **social support** relations are prime examples. You can help someone with their homework or give them personal advice, but this does not *necessarily* mean that that person will return the favor. **Mutuality** or **reciprocity** is not built-in by definition; instead, it must happen as an empirical event in the world. Social networks composed of asymmetric ties are represented by **directed graphs** (or **digraphs**). @fig-directed shows a point-and-line diagram of a digraph, where simple undirected lines are replaced by directed arrows (also called **arcs**). ::: {.cell .fig-cap-location-bottom} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![A directed graph](lesson-graphs-ties_files/figure-html/fig-directed-1.png){#fig-directed width=768} ::: ::: In a directed graph, for every edge, there is a **source node** and a **destination node**. Therefore, *the order in which you list the nodes when you name the edges matters*. The edge $AB$ is a different entity from the edge $BA$. When a digraph has no loops and at most one directed edge connecting a sender to a receiver in each direction, it is called a **simple directed graph**. ### Reciprocity as an Empirical Concept In directed networks, reciprocity is a major analytical focus. For some ties (such as liking, trusting, or friendship), reciprocity is binary; it either exists or it does not. For other ties (such as communication networks built on text volume or call duration), reciprocity is a matter of degree. For instance, you can text someone 10 times a day, but they may text you back only half the time. If @fig-directed were an **advice network** [@cross01], we could say that *H* seeks advice from *D*, but *D* does not seek advice from *H*. This lack of reciprocity is common in formal hierarchies, where advice-seeking often flows upward to more experienced or authoritative actors, reflecting power differentials. In contrast, in a **friendship network**, we would expect a much higher level of reciprocity, as mutual liking is often a defining feature of friendship ties. --- ## Sociological versus Graph-Theoretic Classification of Ties ### Graph-Theoretic Classification of Ties In graph theory, we categorize directed and undirected ties based on their inherent directionality. Figure @fig-graph-theoretic-ties provides a visual summary of these types. ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![A Graph-Theoretic Classification of Ties](lesson-graphs-ties_files/figure-html/fig-graph-theoretic-ties-1.png){#fig-graph-theoretic-ties width=768} ::: ::: * **Symmetric (Undirected)**: Lack meaningful directionality (e.g., "is sibling of"). Represented by **undirected graphs**. * **Asymmetric (Directed)**: Relations that have a natural directionality, represented by **directed graphs**. They split into three flavors: * **Reciprocal**: Edges exist in both directions, indicating mutual interaction (e.g., mutual liking or active email exchange). * **Non-Reciprocal**: An edge exists in only one direction (e.g., sending an email without getting a reply). * **Anti-Reciprocal**: The presence of a tie in one direction logically implies the absence of a tie in the opposite direction (e.g., hierarchical relations like "is boss of"). ### Sociological Classification of Social Ties Sociologists categorize social ties into four main types: **Similarities**, **Social Relations**, **Interactions**, and **Flows**. These four types can be further grouped into **states** (static situations that persist over time, like similarities and social relations) and **events** (repeated behavioral processes that unfold over time, like interactions and flows). Table @tbl-sociological-ties provides a summary. | Category | Type | Description | Examples | |:---------|:---------------------|:----------------------------------------------------------------------------|:---------------------------------------------------------------------------| | **States** | **Similarities** | Connections based on having something in common; typically symmetric. | Propinquity (same school), Memberships (same club), Attributes (same gender). | | | **Social Relations** | Connections based on a culturally recognized role or an affective/cognitive attitude. | **Roles**: Kinship (sibling, parent), Non-Kin (friend, boss).
**Attitudes**: Affective (like, hate), Cognitive (knows, is aware of). | | **Events** | **Interactions** | Regular communication or behavior directed at another person; usually asymmetric. | Communications (texting, calling), Social Support (advice, help), Dominance (bullying, fighting). | | | **Flows** | Transmission of something from one person to another; inherently directed. | Information (gossip, influence), Beliefs, Resources (economic transactions). | : A Sociological Classification of Social Ties {#tbl-sociological-ties} #### Similarities Similarities represent static states where individuals share a common attribute or context. Ties based on similarities are typically symmetric. Examples include *propinquities* (being co-located in a neighborhood), *memberships* (belonging to the same professional organization), and *demographic attributes* (sharing the same age or ethnicity). #### Social Relations Social relations describe culturally recognized roles or cognitive/affective attitudes. These are also static states. They can be symmetric (friendship, sibling) or asymmetric (boss-subordinate, parent-child). Sibling ties are symmetric, while parent/child ties are anti-reciprocal (if *A* is the parent of *B*, *B* cannot be the parent of *A*). Affective ties (liking, trusting, hating) and cognitive ties (knowing of someone, being aware of someone) are inherently asymmetric. #### Interactions Interactions are behavioral events occurring in time. They are asymmetric by default but can be reciprocal. Typical examples include *communications* (texting, calling), *social support* (exchanging advice or lending money), and *dominance* or negative interactions (bullying, physical fighting). #### Flows Flows involve the directed movement of some entity (information, resources, or beliefs) from a sender to a receiver. They are dynamic events that unfold over time and are inherently directional. Examples include the diffusion of *information* (gossip, news, influence) and the transfer of *resources* (economic transactions, disease transmission). --- ## Special Classes of Directed Graphs By imposing structural restrictions on reciprocity, degree, or edge directionality, we can define special classes of directed graphs. ### Symmetric Directed Graphs If, in a directed graph, every pair of connected nodes is linked by a bi-directional, reciprocal relationship, the graph is a **symmetric directed graph**. ::: {.cell .fig-cap-location-bottom} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![A symmetric directed graph](lesson-graphs-ties_files/figure-html/fig-symm-1.png){#fig-symm width=768} ::: ::: @fig-symm shows a symmetric directed graph with eight nodes and sixteen bi-directional edges (thirty-two directed arcs). For every edge from $u$ to $v$, there exists a corresponding edge from $v$ to $u$. ### Functional Graphs A **functional graph** is a special kind of digraph built by imposing the restriction that each node can only have a *single out-neighbor* (i.e., the outdegree of every node is exactly equal to one, $k_{out} = 1$). Functional graphs have important applications in the anthropological analysis of kinship exchange systems in traditional societies [@hageharary96]. ::: {.cell .fig-cap-location-bottom} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![A functional directed graph](lesson-graphs-ties_files/figure-html/fig-func-1.png){#fig-func width=768} ::: ::: @fig-func shows a functional graph with eight nodes. If a graph $G$ is a functional graph, then the number of nodes $V$ is always equal to the number of directed edges $E$ ($V = E = 8$). This is mathematically constrained because each of the $V$ nodes sends out exactly one edge. ### Oriented Graphs {#sec-oriented} An **oriented graph** is a directed graph containing no symmetric (reciprocal) dyads. If there is a directed link from $u$ to $v$, there cannot be a link from $v$ to $u$. It is the structural opposite of a symmetric directed graph. ::: {.cell .fig-cap-location-bottom} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![An oriented directed graph](lesson-graphs-ties_files/figure-html/fig-oriented-1.png){#fig-oriented width=768} ::: ::: In the oriented graph shown in @fig-oriented, every connected pair is linked *only* by a one-way directed tie; reciprocal dyads are forbidden by the nature of the relationship (e.g., strict hierarchy or non-reversible flows). ### Anti-Reciprocal Ties and Directed Tree Graphs As we saw earlier, an asymmetric relation is **anti-reciprocal** if reciprocity is strictly forbidden. If *A* is anti-reciprocally connected to *B*, then *B* *cannot* send the *same type of tie* back to *A*. When these relations are concatenated across multiple nodes, they can form a **directed tree graph** (for a more general consideration of tree graphs see @sec-trees). Consider the relationship "being the father of." You have a father, your father has a father, and so on. This creates a generational lineage represented as a tree. ::: {.cell .fig-cap-location-bottom} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![A tree graph with thirteen nodes](lesson-graphs-ties_files/figure-html/fig-tree-1.png){#fig-tree width=768} ::: ::: In @fig-tree, node $A$ is the earliest common ancestor, and all other nodes are anti-reciprocally related to it. Similarly, formal organizational structures where subordinates "take orders from" a single supervisor generate tree graphs. A notable property of tree graphs is that every node (except the root) has exactly one in-neighbor (one supervisor or one father), but can have multiple out-neighbors (children or subordinates). --- ## Real-World Structural Overlays In real-world settings, simple graph models are often combined to capture the rich social environments of families, organizations, and communities. * **Hierarchies in Organizations**: Formal organizations overlay distinct tie types: * **Same-level ties** (e.g., coworkers, office mates) are typically **symmetric**, implying parity and equality. * **Cross-level ties** (e.g., supervisor-subordinate) are **anti-reciprocal** and **oriented**, representing vertical authority. These ties are often transitive: if *A* is the boss of *B*, and *B* is the boss of *C*, then *A* is also effectively the boss of *C*. * **Kinship Networks in Families**: Family structures mirror this logic: * **Same-generation ties** (e.g., siblings, cousins) are **symmetric**. * **Cross-generation ties** (e.g., parent-of, uncle-of) are **anti-reciprocal** and transitive. ### Multiplexity in Social Relations In actual social networks, actors are rarely linked by only one relationship. **Multiplexity** refers to the presence of multiple, distinct types of ties linking the same pair of nodes simultaneously. For example, two individuals in an office might be linked by a formal, anti-reciprocal role relationship (supervisor and employee) and also by an informal, asymmetric sentiment tie (mutual friendship or liking). Multiplexity adds rich, multi-layered complexity to networks, as the behavior or pattern in one relation (e.g., friendship) often heavily influences or moderates another (e.g., work productivity). ### The Growth of Social Networks Social networks are highly dynamic. They grow and evolve as new ties form, often linking previously separate network structures. A classic example is the formation of a new family unit. A romantic tie (an asymmetric, non-kin relation) between two individuals from separate families can culminate in a marriage tie (a symmetric, kin relation). This single event triggers a cascade of new "in-law" ties (both symmetric same-generation ties and anti-reciprocal cross-generation ties). This effectively merges two separate kinship trees into a highly complex, interconnected network structure. --- ## References {.unnumbered}
